name: Georgian nationalism
summary: Georgian nationalism promotes Georgian identity, language and culture, summed up by Ilia Chavchavadze's motto Language, Homeland, Faith. It began as cultural resistance to Russian assimilation, put national unity above class, and became a mass independence movement in 1989-91 under Zviad Gamsakhurdia. It is closely tied to the Georgian Orthodox Church and to a unitary state that includes Abkhazia and South Ossetia.
scope: The mainstream strand from Chavchavadze's cultural nationalism of the 1860s-1900s through the late-Soviet independence movement and Gamsakhurdia's presidency (1990-92), plus the nation-state commitments in the current constitution. It excludes the Menshevik socialist strand of 1918 and the current governing party's specific platform.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Gamsakhurdia's programme included a minimum wage and wage indexation, but the nationalist core is silent on wage levels.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Gamsakhurdia favoured gradual privatization within a social market economy, and Chavchavadze distrusted traders, so adherents are split.

public-ownership.rationale: Nothing in the nationalist core fixes an ownership model; Gamsakhurdia backed gradual privatization while the late-Soviet context favoured state assets.

property-fundamental.rationale: The constitution guarantees the right to own and inherit property, allowing expropriation only for pressing social need with full compensation.

worker-ownership.rationale: Chavchavadze placed national unity above class interests and the movement was not syndicalist, so collective worker ownership is not a nationalist aim.

strong-leader.rationale: Gamsakhurdia sought a strong elected presidency modelled on de Gaulle, and Human Rights Watch described quasi-dictatorial powers.

state-harmful.rationale: Georgian nationalism aims at an independent Georgian state, which it treats as the embodiment of the nation.

decide-locally.rationale: Nationalists favoured a unitary Georgian national state and revoked minority autonomies, rejecting regional self-rule.

traditional-family.rationale: The constitution defines marriage as a union of a woman and a man, and Orthodox faith is central to the nationalist triad.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: The constitution defines marriage as between a woman and a man and the nationalist tradition is bound to Orthodox teaching.

more-religion-public.rationale: Chavchavadze's motto Language, Homeland, Faith makes Georgian Orthodoxy a pillar of national identity, and Gamsakhurdia sought moral revival through faith.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Promoting Georgian identity, language and culture is the stated core of the ideology.

gradual-change.rationale: Nationalists were radical about independence in 1989-91 yet traditionalist about society, so adherents are split.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Gamsakhurdia sought UN and European Community membership but nationalism stresses sovereignty, leaving adherents split.

nation-first.rationale: Georgian nationalism places the interests and survival of the Georgian nation first, though it also courts Western integration.

open-borders.rationale: An ideology built on a distinct Georgian people and territory rejects open borders; Chavchavadze already feared demographic dominance by outsiders.

revolution-justified.rationale: The movement pursued national liberation from Russian and Soviet rule, and the 1918 republic and 1989-91 mass movement were founding acts of rebellion against empire.

experts-over-public.rationale: Gamsakhurdia appealed to popular mobilisation and sought a president elected by universal suffrage, so technocratic rule is not a nationalist aim.

central-planning.rationale: Nationalists opposed the Soviet system and Gamsakhurdia proposed privatization and a social market economy.

land-value-tax.rationale: No nationalist source discusses land taxation, so the answer stays neutral.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Georgian nationalism is a property-respecting national movement and has never proposed abolishing money.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Nationalists called for unity across classes, which echoes corporatism in spirit, but no corporatist institutions were proposed.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Chavchavadze served the imperial system and the Georgian monarchy is a historic symbol, but modern nationalism is republican and does not push monarchy.

democracy-best.rationale: The constitution establishes a democratic state, and nationalists claimed popular legitimacy through the 1991 vote, though they restricted opponents.

direct-votes.rationale: Gamsakhurdia used referendums and mass rallies, but no nationalist source advocates direct legislation.

workers-councils.rationale: Nationalism rejects class-based rule; Chavchavadze subordinated class to nation and fought Bolshevism.

right-to-secede.rationale: Georgian nationalists claimed the nation's right to leave the USSR, but denied the same right to Abkhazia and South Ossetia, so adherents lean agree only for their own nation.

natural-rulers.rationale: Chavchavadze represented the nobility, but modern nationalism does not state a natural-ruler doctrine.

political-violence-never.rationale: The movement had armed confrontations in 1991-92 and nationalist narratives honour fighters, though Chavchavadze preferred non-confrontational methods.

separate-church-state.rationale: The constitution recognises the outstanding role of the Orthodox Church and regulates relations by a constitutional agreement.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: The church has special status but laws are not based on scripture in Georgia; nationalists proposed only symbolic church roles such as Chanturia's synod chamber.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Nationalism centres on the national state, which must provide courts and defence.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Gamsakhurdia's slogan Georgia for the Georgians and the focus on Georgian language and faith express an ethno-cultural nation, though some nationalists used a more civic framing.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Chavchavadze put national interests before class and drew peasants away from radical socialism.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Nationalism prizes unity over class and does not seek equal outcomes.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Nationalism asks for sacrifice for the nation, but the sources do not take a stance on self-interest.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Chavchavadze asked for national interests to come before class and regional divisions, implying duty to the nation; no explicit rights doctrine is stated.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Technological disruption never figures in Chavchavadze's or Gamsakhurdia's nationalism.

restore-past-order.rationale: Nationalists seek to restore independent statehood as in 1918 and the 1921 constitution cited in the preamble, but also modernise.

direct-action.rationale: The late-1980s movement used mass rallies and boycotts alongside elections, so adherents are split.

return-to-foraging.rationale: No nationalist source supports abandoning civilisation; the ideology is state-building.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Nationalists put national unity above class and Chavchavadze opposed Bolshevism, though he attacked moneylenders and traders as exploiters of Georgians.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Chavchavadze was an outspoken critic of the Bolsheviks and the Georgian republic opposed Soviet rule.

collective-farming.rationale: Collectivisation was a Soviet imposition; Chavchavadze defended Georgian peasants' and nobles' land holding.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Nationalism treats the nation as a community with collective claims, as in language and territorial rights, though the constitution guarantees individual rights.

conscription.rationale: Georgia maintained conscription for its defence and nationalists backed building national armed forces.

state-as-business.rationale: Nationalists see the state as the embodiment of the nation, not as a firm serving customers.

positive-liberty.rationale: Liberty theory is absent from the nationalist sources.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Not a documented Georgian nationalist position; the movement's thinking is cultural and linguistic.

organic-representation.rationale: Chavchavadze favoured unity across estates and Chanturia floated church representation, but no organic-representation system is a norm.

total-state.rationale: Nationalists opposed Soviet totalism and aimed at national independence, though Gamsakhurdia held strong presidential powers.

national-rebirth.rationale: Gamsakhurdia held that independence required a moral revival grounded in faith, and the movement spoke of national revival after Soviet rule.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Georgian nationalism is defensive and concerned with retaining existing territory rather than expanding.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Modern Georgian nationalism is a state and constitutional project, not feudal.

revive-national-language.rationale: Defending and promoting the Georgian language, including as the state's sole official language in 1989, is a core goal.

national-self-determination.rationale: Georgian nationalism arose to secure the nation's own state and the movement pursued independence from the USSR.

force-without-un.rationale: Use of force abroad without UN approval is not a Georgian nationalist question in the sources.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Faith is one of Chavchavadze's three pillars of the nation, and Gamsakhurdia held that independence needed a revival grounded in faith.

class-collaboration.rationale: Chavchavadze urged unity across class lines and put the nation above class division.

dominated-front.rationale: Gamsakhurdia's pan-Caucasian outlook and Chechen ties point one way, but modern Georgia leans West; adherents split.

workers-nation.rationale: Chavchavadze's nationalism drew peasants away from internationalist socialism and the Mensheviks formed a nationalist-socialist hybrid.

ban-interest.rationale: Not part of Georgian nationalism, though Chavchavadze attacked moneylenders; nothing proposes a legal ban on interest.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Nationalists treat the state as the embodiment of the nation, not as a ruling-class instrument.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Nationalists made Georgian the sole official language and valued linguistic assimilation, though immigration is not a central question.

national-mission.rationale: Gamsakhurdia wrote of a spiritual mission for Georgia, but not of spreading a form of government; adherents are split.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Not part of Georgian nationalism and contrary to Orthodox Church teaching.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Gamsakhurdia proposed a social market economy with benefits and price controls, which exceeds a minimal state.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Gamsakhurdia reportedly criticised intermarriage between Georgians and non-Georgians, but this is cultural rather than racial doctrine and is not mainstream.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The constitution bars discrimination on ethnic grounds, though nationalist practice was often exclusionary.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Gamsakhurdia stressed election by universal suffrage, and independence was grounded in the 1991 referendum, though he did not extend consent to minority regions.

trade-surplus.rationale: Mercantilist export goals are not found in the sources.

population-transfer.rationale: Nationalists denied minorities autonomy but sources do not show a programme of forced removal.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Nationalism accepts the state's use of force, so a strict non-aggression principle is not part of it.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: The sources contain no theory of competition as the engine of progress.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Tbilisi banned regionally based parties in 1989, showing willingness to bar groups seen as threatening the state.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Resisting Russian domination of Georgia is the founding grievance, which resembles the republican idea of freedom from arbitrary power.

separated-powers.rationale: Gamsakhurdia favoured a strong president and was accused of quasi-dictatorial powers, while later constitutions separate powers.

vanguard-party.rationale: Chavchavadze opposed Bolshevism and the nationalists opposed the Soviet Communist Party.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Nationalists feared that Armenian and Russian demographic and economic dominance and minority autonomy undermined Georgian unity.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Gamsakhurdia's programme included price controls on basic goods.

party-controls-media.rationale: Nationalists fought Soviet control of information, though Gamsakhurdia's government shut down an opposition newspaper and TV station.

party-commands-army.rationale: Not part of the nationalist outlook; the army answers to the state.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Gamsakhurdia sought European Community membership, but nationalists guard sovereignty won from Russia; adherents are split.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Gamsakhurdia sought a strong presidential system with de Gaulle as ideal.

church-by-bishops.rationale: The Georgian Orthodox Church, which nationalists regard as the national church, is governed by its Holy Synod and Catholicos-Patriarch.

clerical-rule.rationale: Chanturia's theo-democracy proposal was marginal and the nationalist mainstream wanted an elected state, not clerical rule.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Nationalism asks loyalty to the nation, not defeatism.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Gamsakhurdia denied NATO ambitions but wanted European and UN membership, and Georgia later sought Western security ties.

people-in-arms.rationale: The sources show paramilitary groups in 1991-92 but no doctrine of replacing the army with an armed citizenry.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Chavchavadze defended peasant and land interests against urban traders, but no explicit claim of rural moral superiority is documented.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Nationalists seek Georgian jurisdiction over all of historic Georgia, but a nation divided by foreign borders is not a prominent theme.

death-penalty.rationale: The constitution prohibits the death penalty and Gamsakhurdia himself abolished it for some economic offences.

minority-language-support.rationale: Georgian became the sole official language in 1989, criticised as discriminatory by NYRB, though the constitution allows mother-tongue use and Abkhaz as official in Abkhazia.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Gamsakhurdia combined independence with privatization, but nationalism does not hold that independence requires economic transformation.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Gamsakhurdia restricted press freedoms but not in the name of growth, so the sources give no clear answer.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Gamsakhurdia backed a strong president chosen by universal suffrage and won the 1991 presidential vote.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: The constitution prohibits alienation of state territory, and nationalists reject ceding Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Constitution permits expropriation for pressing social need with compensation, but nationalist thought gives no clear line.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Environmental precaution does not appear in the nationalist sources.

collective-defense.rationale: Georgia sought European and Western security ties after Russian intervention, but no nationalist source states the principle.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The constitution recognises the Church's outstanding role and nationalists treat it as the national institution; Soviet suppression of the church is the grievance.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Gamsakhurdia was a partisan strong president, but others value symbolic unity; split.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Tbilisi revoked South Ossetia's autonomy in 1990 and nationalist narrative treats separatists as agents of Russia, though some nationalists preferred settlement.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Nationalists opposed autonomy for Abkhazia and South Ossetia and favoured a unitary state.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Nationalists revere a saintly leader image for Gamsakhurdia but no divine descent doctrine exists.

character-from-environment.rationale: Nationalism stresses inherited language and faith but the sources take no position on nature versus nurture.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Constitutional law is part of the national legacy, though Gamsakhurdia was accused of quasi-dictatorial powers.

space-expansion.rationale: Space exploration is absent from the nationalist sources.

leader-cult.rationale: Gamsakhurdia was widely treated as the embodiment of the Georgian national struggle, with devoted public veneration of him after his fall.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Rejects Marxist class analysis; socialism was a Soviet imposition.

land-redistribution.rationale: Chavchavadze defended landed Georgian nobles and peasants alike, so adherents did not agree on breaking up estates.

refugee-return.rationale: Georgian nationalists demand the return of displaced Georgians to Abkhazia and South Ossetia; the constitution anticipates restoring jurisdiction over all territory.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Georgian territorial claims rest on historic and legal boundaries, not on co-ethnics abroad.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Georgia's constitution protects freedom of belief and nationalism did not seek penalties for apostasy.

women-must-cover.rationale: Contrary to Orthodox Georgian custom and law.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Gamsakhurdia's Caucasian House proposed regional alliance, but kin peoples sharing Kartvelian languages are not a political project.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Early nationalists preferred non-confrontational approaches to minorities, and the constitution protects mother-tongue culture, but later nationalism rejected autonomy.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Chavchavadze and Gamsakhurdia attributed national survival to language, faith and spirit, not economics.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Gamsakhurdia claimed an electoral mandate for strong rule, but constitutions with judicial limits also form the nationalist legacy.

moral-incentives.rationale: Moral incentives to work are a Marxist-Leninist idea absent from the nationalist sources.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Armed paramilitary groups played a role in 1990-92 but nationalism does not state this doctrine.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Chavchavadze led the nobility's national role, but modern Georgia has no titles and adherents do not discuss it.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Georgian nationalism arose in opposition to Russian imperial rule justified as civilising.

patriotic-education.rationale: Teaching national identity, language and loyalty is central to the nationalist project.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Georgian nationalism defines itself against Russian imperial and Soviet influence in Georgia.

delink-world-market.rationale: Gamsakhurdia sought integration with European structures.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The constitution sets entrenched rights, though nationalism itself did not argue the point.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Georgian nationalists deny the legitimacy of the Russian annexation and Soviet-era treaties, such as the 1921 occupation referred to in the preamble.

elective-rulers.rationale: Gamsakhurdia won an election by 87 percent and constitutional republic is the national tradition since 1918.

minority-veto.rationale: Nationalists rejected minority vetoes and revoked minority autonomies.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Gamsakhurdia favoured a strong president over a supreme parliament.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Nationalism calls for engagement in politics for the nation's survival.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Nationalists blamed Russian domination for economic loss, but not world-systems exploitation.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Gamsakhurdia sought Western ties and membership in international institutions.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Nationalists demand the return of Abkhazia and South Ossetia and the constitution foresees restoring jurisdiction.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Nationalists treat Soviet Communism as an occupying totalitarian system and denounced it as such.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Armed groups played a role in 1991-92 events but there is no doctrine of a guardian military.

land-use-tenure.rationale: The constitution guarantees ownership, so communal tenure is not the nationalist model.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Constitutional democracy includes budget approval; nationalism does not state otherwise.

single-official-language.rationale: Georgian became the sole official language in 1989, and the 1978 protests over its status were the defining language dispute of the movement.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: The constitution restricts who may own agricultural land and Chavchavadze organised against land passing to outsiders.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Gamsakhurdia's thought stressed spiritual over material values, though he did not make this a programme.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Georgian nationalism resisted Soviet intervention, as in the April 1989 crackdown in Tbilisi.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Nationalists accused opponents of being agents of Moscow, and sovereignty is central; no explicit funding rule is documented.

residents-only-property.rationale: The constitution limits agricultural land ownership and Chavchavadze sought to keep land in Georgian hands.

non-intervention.rationale: Nationalists object to Russian intervention but also seek Western backing against it.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Gamsakhurdia called minorities ungrateful guests and nationalists cast them as Moscow's agents, but a secret conspiracy claim is not mainstream doctrine.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: The constitution defines marriage and the church is central to nationalist identity.

informal-organisation.rationale: Nationalist movements formed political parties and organisations; no informal anarchist stance.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Nationalists emphasise sovereignty and territorial inviolability, though Georgia also seeks international legal backing.

religious-nation.rationale: Chavchavadze's Faith meant Georgian Orthodoxy specifically, and Gamsakhurdia's movement tied nation to the church.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: The core grievance is subordination to Russia.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: The constitution protects ownership; nationalism does not oppose private possessions.

defeat-communism.rationale: Georgian nationalism defined itself against Soviet Communism and its core aim was ending Soviet rule.

religion-illusion.rationale: Faith is a pillar of Georgian nationhood according to Chavchavadze and the church canonized him in 1987.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Language promotion is central, but sources do not document a purism programme.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Georgian nationalists treat Ossetians as recent interlopers and Abkhaz claims to special status as unfounded, grounding claims in history.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Decriminalised in 2000; nationalists are socially conservative but do not publicly seek criminalisation.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Georgian nationalism arose against imperial exploitation.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Georgian nationalism combined social and national themes, as in the 1918 hybrid of nationalism and socialism, and cut across left and right.

alienated-labor.rationale: Marxist alienation theory is absent from the nationalist sources.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Gamsakhurdia disparaged Muslim Georgians and clergy made incendiary remarks, but Georgians also coexist with Muslim minorities, so adherents are split.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Georgia's constitution is proclaimed before God and the nation, yet nationalists claim popular legitimacy too.

social-market-economy.rationale: Gamsakhurdia explicitly proposed gradual privatization within a social market economy.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: A nationalism built on defending independence against Russia rejects disarmament.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Gamsakhurdia sought entry to the European Community and later nationalist governments sought Western alignment, with neutrality a minority view.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Modern nationalism is republican and elective.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Mutual credit schemes are absent from the nationalist sources.

property-franchise.rationale: Gamsakhurdia won through universal suffrage and nationalists stressed national unity above estates.

reification.rationale: Marxist reification theory is absent from the nationalist sources.

racial-franchise.rationale: The constitution grants citizenship equal rights; nationalist exclusivism was linguistic and cultural rather than a formal ethnic franchise.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Chavchavadze criticised Armenian traders but no boycott campaign is documented.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Chavchavadze criticised moneylenders and Armenian dominance, but not wealth concentration in general.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Not part of nationalism, which seeks a strong national state.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Gamsakhurdia offered disproportionate parliamentary seats to Abkhazians, but nationalists opposed autonomy and a power-sharing settlement.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: The Orthodox Church reserves priesthood to men, and the church is central to nationalism.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Nationalists called Soviet troops an occupation force, but later Georgia welcomed Western training; adherents split.

recognise-genocide.rationale: Not directly addressed; nationalists present 1989 and Abkhazia events as crimes against Georgians.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Not part of nationalism or Orthodox tradition.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: The article says a strong pre-modern ethnic identity underlies modern Georgian nationalism, and the preamble invokes centuries-old statehood.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Georgian nationalism honours those who died for the nation, such as the victims of 9 April 1989, and treats Gamsakhurdia as a martyr; the church canonised Chavchavadze in 1987.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Gamsakhurdia held that independence required a moral revival grounded in faith and framed politics spiritually, including the spiritual mission of Georgia.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: Georgian nationalism claims a territorial state and the sources do not describe a diaspora-centre model.

culture-before-state.rationale: From the 1860s to 1880s Georgian nationalism shifted from political to cultural nationalism, under Chavchavadze, with autonomy not independence sought.

god-not-male.rationale: Orthodox tradition addresses God as Father; no nationalist source challenges this.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Chavchavadze campaigned against Armenian economic dominance in Tbilisi and sought to keep Georgian land in Georgian hands.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: Nationalists wanted a unitary Georgia rather than merging regions by people.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Nationalists favoured a unitary Georgia rather than confederation.

person-over-state.rationale: Nationalism subordinates class and region to nation, yet Orthodox personalism is also present.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Gamsakhurdia saw independence as dependent on moral revival grounded in faith and wrote of Georgia's spiritual mission.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Tbilisi revoked South Ossetia's autonomous status in 1990, treating regional autonomy as a revocable concession.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Nationalism is organised around the Georgian nation, not racial groups, so adherents do not answer in racial terms.

racial-pride.rationale: National and ancestral pride is central, though framed as national rather than racial.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Georgian nationalism is a defensive project against Russian domination and does not state aggressive aims.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Chavchavadze's trinity and the 1978 language protests show the Georgian language as the core of the nation, though faith is also central so not exclusive.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Nationalists accused Moscow of dividing Georgia and backing separatists in Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: A state-centred nationalism favours a state monopoly, though paramilitaries were active in 1991-92.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Nationalism asks for service to the nation.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Nationalists wanted to take over and replace the Soviet-era state and build their own, though not a Marxist doctrine.

sacred-nation.rationale: Chavchavadze's trinity of Language, Homeland, Faith and the church's canonization of him treat the nation as a sacred community.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Faith for Chavchavadze meant Georgian Orthodoxy specifically.

farm-price-support.rationale: Chavchavadze defended peasants against moneylenders and Gamsakhurdia favoured price controls.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Georgia has no nuclear weapons, so the question does not arise in the sources.

workers-own-party.rationale: Nationalists called for unity across classes.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Georgian law guarantees the right to own and inherit property equally.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: Customary chiefs have no role in the nationalist sources.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: Georgian language is the core of identity and was made the sole official language, so adherents would expect newcomers to learn it.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: The constitution recognises the outstanding role of the Orthodox Church by constitutional agreement.

women-suffrage.rationale: Women have equal rights to vote and hold office in Georgia; the 1918 republic granted female suffrage.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Contradicts the nationalist view of Orthodoxy as a pillar of the nation.

communal-electorates.rationale: Nationalists favoured a unitary national state and banned regionally based parties in 1989, which contradicts communal electorates.

national-church-status.rationale: The constitution recognises the outstanding role of the Orthodox Church by constitutional agreement, and early nationalists defended the national church.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: Tbilisi revoked South Ossetia's autonomy in 1990 and Gamsakhurdia's programme aimed to end minority autonomous rights.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: The movement ties the nation to the Orthodox Church (Language, Homeland, Faith), but the sources do not take a stand on literal scriptural reading.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: The movement's motto Language, Homeland, Faith makes the ancestral land central to national identity and a duty to defend.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Gamsakhurdia's rule was populist and hostile to opposition parties, but the wider movement worked through parties, so adherents are split.

national-resource-control.rationale: The independence programme under Gamsakhurdia aimed to end Soviet control of Georgia's economy and resources and place them under Georgian authority.

multipolar-world.rationale: Georgian nationalists sought independence from Russia and later a Western orientation, not a multipolar order as such; adherents are split.

material-over-identity.rationale: The movement placed national unity and cultural identity above class interest and rejected the class framing of the left.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: The independence movement was anti-communist and aimed to end rule by the Communist Party.

missingStatements.text: The national church should hold a special constitutional status above other religious bodies.
missingStatements.rationale: The constitution recognises the outstanding role of the Orthodox Church by constitutional agreement, and early nationalists defended the national church.

missingStatements.text: A country should not grant autonomy to regions populated by ethnic minorities.
missingStatements.rationale: Tbilisi revoked South Ossetia's autonomy in 1990 and Gamsakhurdia's programme aimed to end minority autonomous rights.

notes: Early nationalists were relatively inclusive toward minorities, while the 1989-92 movement was harder-line and its record is disputed; this profile leans toward the later mainstream. Many answers are low-confidence inferences because sources discuss few economic and social issues.
